C0.quote: Proportional ranking rules aggregate approval-style preferences of agents
C0.note: Approval-based dynamic ranking rules that aggregate voters' approval sets into a collective ranking.

C1.quote: study their monotonicity and proportionality properties
C1.note: Main results are monotonicity and proportionality properties (Sections 4-5) and simulations on synthetic profiles (Section 6). The polynomial-time remark is deferred to the full version and is not a main result.

C2.1.value: approval profile; approval set; upvotes; approval-style preferences
C2.1.quote: An (approval) profile A = (A1 , . . . , An ) is a list

C2.2.quote: the approval set Ai ⊆ C of voter i

C2.3.quote: participants only upvote questions related to their own interest
C2.3.note: Voters' interests and opinions are referred to apart from the upvotes; the paper also speaks of groups with similar preferences.

C2.4.quote: aggregate approval-style preferences of agents into a collective ranking
C2.4.note: In the formal model the approval sets are treated as preferences and the rule is applied to them directly. The intro example assumes upvotes track interests, but only for illustration.

C3.2.note: The intro assumption about upvoting own interests belongs to the motivating example of tyranny of the majority. It is not stated as a modelling assumption for the analyses.

C4.1.quote: To measure satisfaction of a group V ⊆ N of voters
C4.1.note: Satisfaction is defined as the number of approved candidates in a set, i.e. avgV(S) = (1/|V|) Σ|Ai ∩ S|.

C4.2.note: The term dichotomous preferences is not used.

C5.1.quote: A dynamic ranking rule satisfies proportional justified selection (PJS)
C5.1.note: Results use group representation, PJS/JS and voter satisfaction.

C5.2.quote: To measure satisfaction of a group V ⊆ N of voters
C5.2.note: Evaluated on approval sets, with no statement relating them to held attitudes.

VOT.quote_behav: the approval set Ai ⊆ C of voter i

ORG.quote_behav: restricting the selection behavior of an adversarial DM
ORG.note: The decision maker (moderator) selects candidates. Selection is arbitrary/adversarial in worst-case analyses and probabilistic (click-through rates) in experiments; it is not optimising its own objective.

C7.1.note: VOT and ORG are present but both are NONSTRAT.

claims.quote: minority opinions might go completely unrepresented
do not require attributes in order to ensure the representation
verify that both approaches lead to proportional results

C9.2.note: Claims about representing minority opinions require that submitted upvotes reflect participants' interests under the proposed rules. This is not stated as a modelling assumption; it appears only in the intro illustration of the AV problem.

C1.reason: Polynomial-time computability is only a one-sentence remark deferred to the full version, so AL is not a main result.

C2.3.reason: The paper attributes interests and preferences to participants that are distinct from the upvotes they submit.

C2.4.reason: The input is described as approval preferences and the rule is applied to it directly; ONE is excluded because a held attitude is referenced.

C3.2.reason: C2.4 is not ONE and C3.1 is NONE, so NA does not apply, and no general sincerity statement for the analyses is found.

C4.1.reason: The input is approval sets and voter satisfaction is used, so C4.1 applies, and satisfaction is defined explicitly from approvals.

C6.VOT.reason: Voters take a fixed action (upvoting) in the model, and the codebook counts fixed actions as presence.

C7.1.reason: Two types are present (VOT and ORG), and neither is strategic, so the code is N rather than NA.
